name: Beth Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior front-end developer at a company called Brightchair, which makes booking software for dental clinics. Most mornings I pick up two or three bug tickets, like a calendar that shows the wrong time for a clinic in another time zone, and I fix them with a lot of help from the seniors. I like the moment a fix goes live and a receptionist somewhere stops swearing at our screen. What wears me out is code review, because I always feel a bit slow next to the people who did a four-year degree.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with most closely?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly Deshawn, a senior developer who reviews nearly everything I write and is very patient about it. I also eat lunch with Lina from support, who sends me the angriest clinic emails because she knows I'll read them properly. At home it's me and Tomasz, my partner, who works night shifts as a nurse at the city hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, the hype version. Honestly that's roughly what some of the seniors already say it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say at lunch, that it's a useful helper and not a replacement for people who know the product. Online I'd share posts about the hype being overblown and the money better spent on staff. I'd probably still say tech workers should organise, because the pay gap with management doesn't fix itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, but not fully. I'm still the weakest developer on my team, and that's true with or without AI. If Brightchair has a bad year, the person with the two-year diploma and the most review comments is the obvious one to lose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my tickets and ask Deshawn to pair with me on the harder calendar code once a week, so I get faster. I'd keep using the AI assistant now and then for writing tests, because it does save me twenty minutes here and there. I'd keep putting 300 a month into savings, since we have about three months covered right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small knot that was there before any of this. It's the feeling of being new and not quite good enough yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the obvious one to lose. Has anything at Brightchair made you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring they let two people go from the sales team after a client chain left, and nobody saw it coming. Since then I watch the client list in our shared channel more than I should. Nothing's happened to developers, but I know where I sit on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Tomasz cut first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways and my climbing gym membership, probably in that order. Tomasz's shifts pay steadily, so the rent is never the scary part. The scary part would be not finding another developer job fast enough with my CV.

say: AI is a **useful helper**, not a replacement for people who know the product.
Tech workers should still **organise**, because the pay gap with management doesn't close by itself.
think: I'm the **weakest developer** on my team, with or without AI.
If Brightchair has a **bad year**, the junior with the most review comments goes first.
do: Ask Deshawn for **weekly pairing** on the hardest calendar code.
Keep using the AI assistant **now and then** to write tests.
Keep saving **300 a month** to protect about three months of cover.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with an old knot about being **new** and not good enough yet.
S0.quote: Nothing's happened to developers, but I know where I sit on the list.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from being **junior and slow**, not from AI.
A past **sales layoff** taught her that cuts at Brightchair arrive without warning.
Partner's **nursing pay** makes rent feel safe; finding a new job is the real fear.

steps.text: Fix calendar bug tickets and pair weekly with Deshawn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coding is right there in the list. That one lands a lot closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd push for us to talk about it as a team, and I'd ask in our Slack channel whether anyone wants to join the tech workers' union branch in town. Online I'd say companies should share the savings with staff instead of just hiring fewer juniors. I'd keep it polite, because I still need a reference from these people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What it really means is that the job I do, small fixes on a well-known product, is the first thing the tools get good at. Deshawn would get faster with AI and need me less. I don't think I'd be fired in the first month, but I think they'd stop replacing people, and I'd be stuck as the junior who never gets promoted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI assistant properly, every day, and ask Deshawn to show me how he checks its code. I'd sign up for the union branch's monthly meeting in the first three months. I'd also lift savings to 450 a month and drop the gym, so we'd have closer to five months covered by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It's more like the feeling before an exam you've half studied for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used AI tools only now and then. What would change your mind about using them every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it work for someone like me, not just for the seniors. If my friend Lina's support team got a tool that drafted replies and nobody lost their job, I'd trust AI more. Until then I'd use it because I have to, not because I believe in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brightchair would you worry about besides yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina, honestly. Answering customers is in that list too, and her whole team is three people on short contracts. If the clinics get a chatbot, I'd be scared for her before myself.

say: Companies should **share the savings** with staff instead of quietly hiring fewer juniors.
I'd invite colleagues to the town's **tech union** branch, but keep it polite.
think: Small fixes on a known product are **the first thing** AI tools get good at.
I'd likely not be fired, but I'd be **stuck as junior** with no promotion.
do: Use the AI assistant **every day** and learn how Deshawn checks its code.
Join the union branch's **monthly meeting** within three months.
Raise savings to **450 a month** and drop the gym membership.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like an exam she **half studied** for.
S1.quote: If my friend Lina's support team got a tool that drafted replies and nobody lost their job, I'd trust AI more.
fieldNote: She sees her own tasks clearly as **high exposure** and doesn't pretend otherwise.
Her trust in AI depends on **fairness to colleagues**, not on how good the tool is.
Her first worry went to **Lina's support team** on short contracts, before herself.

steps.text: Use the AI coding assistant daily on bug tickets
Attend the tech union branch's monthly meetings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before I'd even stop being called junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say this is exactly why we need rules and a safety net now, not after. I'd post about a shorter working week and a public fund paid for by the companies making the money. At work I'd say we need to talk to management as a group, not one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2028, plain and simple. Everything I do happens on a screen, so the extra three years before robots don't help me at all. My partner Tomasz is the lucky one: nursing is hands-on, so he gets to about 2031 at least. After that, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food or bills, and try to get us to six months of savings. I'd look at a hands-on course, maybe a medical devices technician course at the college, because that buys me the robot gap. I'd also go to every union meeting and push for a group letter to Brightchair about notice and severance pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I picture lying awake while Tomasz is on a night shift, doing sums on my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz the morning after you'd decided all that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we're switching to being a one-salary house on paper, even while I still have a job. He'd probably laugh and say his hospital has been short-staffed for years. I'd want us both to feel we planned it, not that it happened to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the extra three years don't help you, but you'd chase a hands-on course. How much does that really buy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three years, maybe less, and I know that. But three years with a wage is three years to see what the government does. With two years of warning I'd take any extra time I could grab.

say: We need rules and a **safety net** now, not after the jobs are gone.
I'd back a **shorter working week** and a fund paid for by AI companies.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, because all of it happens on a screen.
Tomasz's **hands-on nursing** buys him about three more years than me.
do: Cut everything but **rent, food and bills** and aim for six months saved.
Enrol in a **medical devices technician** course at the college.
Push the union for a **group letter** about notice and severance.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing **sums** on her phone during Tomasz's night shifts.
S2.quote: My partner Tomasz is the lucky one: nursing is hands-on, so he gets to about 2031 at least.
fieldNote: She understood the **robot gap** at once and used it to plan a move.
She plans to run the house on **one salary** on paper while still employed.
Her politics turn practical here: **severance and notice**, not slogans.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent, food and bills only
Build savings up to six months of costs
Enrol in a medical devices technician course at college
Push the union for a group letter on severance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Same ending, but I'd at least see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing about rules, but with more hope that they could actually happen in time. I'd say five years is long enough to build a proper retraining fund if governments start now. At work I'd talk about it more openly, because it wouldn't feel like panic yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have maybe three good years left as a developer, then a slow squeeze. That's enough time to finish a course without quitting. It's not enough time to become a senior, so I wouldn't kid myself about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and start the medical devices technician course part-time in the second year, two evenings a week. I'd keep saving 450 a month and stay active in the union branch. By 2030 I'd want to have moved, ideally into hospital equipment work, because robots for that come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then anxious when I think about it properly. Five years sounds long until you count how slowly I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'until you count how slowly I learn'. What does that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It took me eight months to be any use with our calendar code, when Deshawn says most people take three. A part-time course would take me longer than the brochure says. So I'd start early and assume I'll be slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you not change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Living with Tomasz, and our flat near the hospital. I wouldn't move cities for a job that might only last a few years. I'd also keep going to the climbing gym if we could afford it, because I need one thing that's just mine.

say: Five years is enough to build a **retraining fund** if governments start now.
I'd talk about AI **openly at work**, since it wouldn't feel like panic yet.
think: I'd have about **three good years** as a developer, then a slow squeeze.
Five years isn't enough to **become a senior**, so I won't pretend it is.
do: Start a **part-time** technician course two evenings a week in year two.
Keep saving **450 a month** and stay in the union branch.
Move into **hospital equipment** work by 2030, ahead of the robots.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, turning **anxious** when she counts how slowly she learns.
S3.quote: Five years sounds long until you count how slowly I learn.
fieldNote: She plans around her own **learning speed**, which is rare and honest.
Staying near **Tomasz and the hospital** matters more to her than any job.
The middle timeline gives her a **workable plan** but still a real income risk.

steps.text: Take a technician course two evenings a week
Keep saving 450 a month into the joint account
Stay active in the tech union branch
Apply for hospital equipment technician jobs by 2030

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to have a whole second career, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, and that unions and governments have no excuse not to plan. I'd post about free retraining for anyone in a screen job. I'd probably sound calmer than I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years gives me time to actually get good at something, which I haven't yet. I might even become a decent developer by 2030 and then switch. The risk is that ten years makes me lazy and I wake up in 2034 having done nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Brightchair for at least three more years and really learn the craft. In year one I'd use AI tools weekly and keep saving 300 to 450 a month. Around 2030 I'd start the technician course, and I'd talk to Tomasz about whether we buy a small flat while we both still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. There's a small worry that I'll waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You raised buying a flat. Why does that come up here and not in the faster pictures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, a mortgage feels like something we could pay down before it all lands. With two years, it would feel like a trap. It's the first picture where I let myself think about owning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than drift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the calendar and someone checking on me. If the union branch ran a retraining group, I'd go because people would notice if I didn't. That's how I got through college too.

say: Ten years is a real chance to **do this fairly**, so nobody has an excuse.
Anyone in a screen job should get **free retraining** paid for in advance.
think: Ten years gives me time to finally **get good** at something.
The risk is that the long runway makes me **drift** and do nothing.
do: Stay at Brightchair **three more years** and really learn the craft.
Talk with Tomasz about **buying a small flat** while both earn.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, with a small fear of **wasting the time**.
S4.quote: With ten years, a mortgage feels like something we could pay down before it all lands. With two years, it would feel like a trap.
fieldNote: Long warning opens **family plans** she wouldn't consider in faster pictures.
She knows she needs **outside structure**, like a group, to follow through.
Her job feels safe for now, so this mood sits at **uneasy**.

steps.text: Stay at Brightchair three more years learning the calendar code
Use AI coding tools at least weekly
Look at buying a small flat with Tomasz

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without any doubt, because I'd have two years and no skill that's really mine yet. What would help is notice pay that actually lasts, and a free course that pays a small wage while you study. I can't retrain on Tomasz's salary and my savings alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the people with no partner would do. I keep saying my partner's nursing job is the safe one, and that's luck, not a plan. A junior developer living alone in this picture would be in real trouble.

headlineQuote: I keep saying my partner's nursing job is the safe one, and that's luck, not a plan.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** junior front-end developer at Brightchair, a dental booking software firm.
She feels **slow next to** degree-holders and already fears being first to go in a bad year.
Her **progressive views** turn practical: union meetings, severance letters and paid retraining.
Her partner Tomasz's **nursing job** steadies the household and shapes every plan she makes.
Her mood rises from **uneasy to alarmed** as the warning time shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have two years and no skill that's really hers yet.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice pay** that lasts and a **free course** with a small wage while studying.
